question: you have just completed the capsulorhexis of your cataract surgery when the eye suddenly becomes tense and you lose the red reflex. The lens starts to move anteriorly. What is the next thing that you should do?

options.A: Finish nuclear removal as quickly as you can
options.B: Inject balanced salt solution to fill the anterior chamber
options.C: Inject viscoelastic, put finger over eye, and then close the wound with a suture
options.D: Perform posterior sclerotomies and flush out anterior chamber

explanation: This patient is experiencing a suprachoroidal hemorrhage (expulsive hemorrhage Recognizing this condition early is crucial. The wound should be closed with a suture as quickly as possible. While awaiting the suture from the scrub tech, you can fill the anterior chamber with viscoelastic. These maneuvers prevent intraocular contents from being expulsed. There is controversy over whether posterior sclerotomies should be performed next. This is based on the surgeon's preference and comfort level with performing posterior sclerotomies. If performed, the sclerotomies should be placed 5-6 mm posterior to the limbus and the cutdown should extend until blood is encountered or the bluish coloration of the choroid is visible. If you are unsure of which quadrant to start, do the inferotemporal quadrant first.

review.explanation: A suddenly rock-hard eye with loss of the red reflex and forward movement of the lens during cataract surgery is a suprachoroidal (expulsive) haemorrhage, and the single priority is to re-establish a closed globe immediately so that intraocular contents are not expelled. Option C bundles the correct immediate manoeuvres: fill the chamber with viscoelastic and apply digital pressure while the suture is being handed over, then close the wound. Continuing phacoemulsification invites expulsion of lens and vitreous, and injecting BSS cannot counteract the rising suprachoroidal pressure. Posterior sclerotomies may be considered, but only after the wound is secure, and their timing and value remain debated.

question: What location for an ocular melanoma has the best prognosis?
explanation: Melanoma of the uveal tract is the most common primary intraocular malignancy in adults Iris melanomas have the best prognosis while melanomas of the ciliary body have the worst. Most uveal melanomas are located in the choroid while the iris is the least common site (~3-10% of all uveal melanomas). The BCSC states that the mortality rate of iris melanomas is approximately 14%; for conjunctival melanomas is 25%; for choroidal melanoma (12-50% depending on tumor size); and 30-50% for ciliary body melanomas.

review.explanation: Iris melanomas carry the best prognosis among uveal melanomas, with metastatic mortality of roughly 5 to 15 percent, because they are visible early and therefore small at detection, are more often spindle cell type, and less frequently carry monosomy 3. Ciliary body melanomas fare worst because they grow silently behind the iris and present late with large tumour volume. Choroidal melanoma sits in between, with prognosis driven mainly by tumour size and cytogenetics. Conjunctival melanoma is not a uveal melanoma at all, and its mortality of roughly 25 percent exceeds that of iris melanoma, so it is not the answer.

question: Infectious crystalline keratopathy has an unusual frosted branch appearance in corneal grafts. Which of the following organisms is most commonly associated with infectious crystalline keratopathy after corneal transplant?
explanation: Infectious crystalline keratopathy (ICK) is characterized by white, branching stromal deposits resembling snowflakes with no or minimal inflammatory signs (e.g. redness, pain). The classic scenario is a patient who has undergone a penetrating keratoplasty (PKP) and is therefore taking chronic topical corticosteroids. The most commonly involved organism is Streptococcus viridans (an alpha-hemolytic Strep species) although other organisms can also cause this entity. Treatment initially consists of topical vancomycin, cessation of corticosteroids, and possible broad spectrum systemic antibiotic use. Cases resistant to treatment may eventually require a repeat PKP. Transcribed from a screenshot in the source document.

review.explanation: Infectious crystalline keratopathy classically appears in a chronically steroid-treated graft as white, branching, needle-like or fernlike stromal opacities with strikingly little surrounding inflammation, and the organism recovered in the majority of cases is viridans group streptococcus. The indolent, non-inflamed picture reflects organisms growing in a biofilm within the stromal lamellae, which shields them from both the host response and topical antibiotics, and topical corticosteroid further blunts the reaction. Staphylococcal species, other streptococci, Haemophilus and even Candida can produce an identical appearance but are considerably less common. Treatment is fortified topical antibiotics such as vancomycin with tapering of the corticosteroid, and repeat keratoplasty in refractory cases.

question: What is the most common quadrant for scleral rupture in an open globe caused by blunt trauma?
explanation: C. According to the BCSC Fundamentals book, the most common site of scleral rupture following blunt trauma is the superonasal quadrant near the limbus. Other sites that are common for scleral rupture following blunt trauma are: - In a circumferential arc parallel to the corneal limbus in the quadrant opposite the side of impact - At the insertion of the rectus muscles - At the equator of the globe Transcribed from a screenshot in the source document.

review.explanation: BCSC gives the superonasal quadrant just posterior to the limbus as the commonest site of scleral rupture after blunt trauma, because the sclera is relatively thin there and most blunt objects strike the globe from the inferotemporal side, producing rupture in the quadrant opposite the impact. Ruptures characteristically run in a circumferential arc parallel to the limbus, and other weak points are just behind the rectus muscle insertions and at the equator. In a previously operated eye the old cataract or keratoplasty wound is the weakest point and gives way first, which is why surgical history matters when you suspect occult rupture.

review.explanation: A posterior subcapsular cataract sits immediately in front of the nodal point, directly on the visual axis, so symptoms are worst when the pupil constricts and the opacity occupies proportionally more of the aperture. That is why glare and haloes in bright sunlight or against oncoming headlights are the complaint patients volunteer most, and why acuity in a dim examination lane can be far better than the patient's real-world function. Near vision is also characteristically reduced more than distance vision, because accommodative miosis brings the opacity fully across the pupil, so both listed symptoms are genuine; glare is the classic single best answer because it is the symptom disproportionate to the measured Snellen acuity.

question: Q-A patient with no significant past ocular history aside from cataract undergoes cataract surgery complicated by vitreous loss. Two months after surgery, the vision deteriorates prompting evaluation in your clinic. An OCT is performed and is pictured above. Based on the history and OCT findings, what is the most likely pathophysiology of this finding?

options.D: Retinal ischemia induced release of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF)

explanation: The OCT demonstrates prominent cystoid macular edema (CME). CME after cataract surgery is also known as Irvine-Gass syndrome. There are many causes for CME including vitreomacular traction, inflammation / uveitis, diabetes, X-linked hereditary retinoschisis, epiretinal membrane, and retinitis pigmentosa. Following cataract surgery the most important influences are inflammatory mediators such as prostaglandins that disrupt blood vessel integrity resulting in leakage of fluid into the macula. Vitreomacular traction (VMT) can occur following vitreous loss during cataract surgery and can cause CME, but there is no evidence of VMT on this OCT. The first treatment for most cases of CME (including post-surgical CME) is medical therapy with topical steroids and topical NSAIDs.

review.explanation: The OCT shows pseudophakic cystoid macular oedema, Irvine-Gass syndrome, which classically appears about 4 to 12 weeks after surgery and is far more likely after a complicated case with vitreous loss. The mechanism is surgical inflammation with prostaglandin-mediated breakdown of the blood-retinal barrier, which is exactly why topical NSAID plus corticosteroid is first-line treatment. Vitreomacular traction can follow vitreous loss and can cause oedema, but the OCT would show a taut hyaloid tenting the fovea, which is absent. Weak intercellular adhesions describes the schisis cavities of X-linked retinoschisis, and ischaemia-driven VEGF release describes diabetic or vein-occlusion oedema, and neither fits an eye with no other ocular history.

Incidentally, the patient is a +6.00 hyperope OU and has a family history of lung cancer. Which of the following conditions is most likely also present in this patient?
explanation: This patient is a high hyperope whose fundus photograph shows an exudative retinal detachment. The FA shows a diffuse "leopard-spot" pattern *without* any leakage. These findings are classic features of "uveal effusion syndrome." (Note: the family history of lung cancer was a red herring to sway you to pick "BDUMP" which is associated with lung cancer and can also have a leopard spot pattern on FA).

review.explanation: Uveal effusion syndrome occurs in nanophthalmic or highly hyperopic eyes whose thickened, abnormal sclera obstructs vortex vein outflow and impedes transscleral egress of protein, producing a shifting exudative retinal detachment. Chronic RPE change then gives the characteristic leopard-spot pattern of alternating hypo- and hyperfluorescence, and the crucial detail is that there is no leakage, which excludes an inflammatory or neovascular cause. BDUMP also produces leopard spotting and is associated with an occult systemic carcinoma, but a family history rather than a personal history of lung cancer is a deliberate red herring, and the +6.00 refraction points firmly to uveal effusion. CAR causes photoreceptor dysfunction with an extinguished ERG rather than an exudative detachment, and multiple sclerosis is unrelated.

question: most important risk factor for the development and progression of diabetic retinopathy?
explanation: Important long-term data on disease rates and progression, including a direct association between longer duration of both type 1 and type 2 diabetes and increased prevalence of diabetic retinopathy, were provided by the WESDR (Wisconsin Epidemiologic Study of Diabetic Retinopathy) Among WESDR participants with a 20-year history of diabetes mellitus, nearly 99% of those with type 1 disease and 60% of those with type 2 disease had some degree of diabetic retinopathy. PDR was also reported in 50% of patients with a 20-year history of type 1 diabetes and in 25% of those with a 25-year history of type 2 diabetes. In addition, a visual acuity of 20/200 or worse was observed in 3.6% of patients with younger-onset disease (ie, aged <30 years at diagnosis) and 1.6% of patients with older-onset disease (ie, aged 30 years or older at diagnosis). This vision loss was attributed to diabetic retinopathy in 86% of the younger-onset group and 33% of the older-onset group. AAO retina

review.explanation: Duration of diabetes is the single strongest predictor of both the presence and the severity of diabetic retinopathy, as the WESDR data showed, with nearly all type 1 patients having some retinopathy after 20 years of disease. Glycaemic control, established by the DCCT and UKPDS, is the most important modifiable risk factor and is what you actually intervene on, but it is not the strongest determinant of who develops retinopathy. Hypertension and hyperlipidaemia are additional modifiable contributors, hypertension particularly to progression and hyperlipidaemia particularly to hard exudate and maculopathy, but both rank below duration and glycaemic control.

The blood supply to the inner layers of the retina is typically derived entirely from the central retinal artery (CRA). The exception is that approximately 1530% of eyes have a cilioretinal artery which is a branch most directly from the posterior ciliary arteries (PCAs). The CRA, PCAs, and lacrimal artery are branches of the ophthalmic artery. Most cases of CRAO are visually-devastating with greater than two-thirds of cases having visual acuity of worse than 20/400. The majority of CRAO cases associated with good central visual acuity are those with a patent cilioretinal artery. Vision of NLP typically does not occur in CRAO, but can occur with simultaneous choroidal infarction (e.g. ophthalmic artery occlusion).

review.explanation: A cilioretinal artery, present in roughly 15 to 30 percent of eyes, arises from the short posterior ciliary circulation, usually via the peripapillary choroid or the circle of Zinn-Haller, rather than from the central retinal artery. That separate origin is precisely why it stays perfused during a central retinal artery occlusion and can preserve central acuity, which matches the described fundus whitening with a spared foveal island and the angiogram showing filling of only those few vessels. The central retinal artery, the posterior ciliary arteries and the lacrimal artery are all branches of the ophthalmic artery, so answering ophthalmic artery is one step too proximal for a question asking which vessel the cilioretinal artery most directly branches from.

question: associated with eye pain worse with eye movement. On exam the patient has 20/60 best corrected vision in the right eye and 20/20 vision in the left eye. She demonstrates an afferent pupillary defect and difficulty with color vision in the right eye. Which of the following tests is the most important to assess her long-term prognosis for development of multiple sclerosis?

options.B: Visual field test to assess for any deficits in the contralateral eye
options.C: MRI of the brain to look for white matter lesions
options.D: MRI of the orbits with IV contrast to confirm enhancement of the right optic nerve

explanation: The Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial (ONTT) showed that the long-term risk for development of multiple sclerosis (MS) can be assessed in patients with isolated optic neuritis based on the presence or absence of characteristic white matter changes on MRI of the brain. A patient with isolated optic neuritis and no characteristic white matter changes on MRI of the brain has a 22% risk of MS development in 10 years. This risk climbs to 56% in 10 years for patients with one or more white matter lesions. The 10-year risk for MS development among all patients with a single bout of clinically isolated optic neuritis (not taking into account MRI findings) is 38%. This information can be remembered as the "10/20/40/60 rule." MRI of the orbits is often performed in patients with atypical presentations of optic neuritis, but is not necessary for the clinical diagnosis of optic neuritis and has no bearing on prognosis for development of MS. Assessment for subclinical involvement of the contralateral eye in a patient with apparent monocular optic neuritis likewise does not aid in prediction of MS formation. More information regarding the ONTT findings (15-year data): The ONTT enrolled patients between 1988 and 1991 and followed them prospectively for 15 years. The 15-year data found the following: - The probability of developing MS by 15 years after an episode of optic neuritis was 50%. - If no lesions were found on baseline brain MRI, then the risk was 25% over 15 years. - If one or more lesions were found on baseline brain MRI, then the risk was 72% over 15 years. Optic Neuritis Study Group. Multiple sclerosis risk after optic neuritis: final optic neuritis treatment trial follow-up. Arch Neurol. 2008;65:727-32.

review.explanation: The Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial established that the number of demyelinating white matter lesions on brain MRI at presentation is the strongest predictor of conversion to multiple sclerosis: about 22 percent at 10 years with no lesions versus about 56 percent with one or more, against an overall 10-year risk near 38 percent. That is why brain MRI is obtained in every case of typical optic neuritis, and it is now also the basis for deciding on disease-modifying therapy. Orbital MRI may show enhancement of the affected nerve but only confirms a diagnosis that is already clinical and carries no prognostic weight. Family history modifies risk only slightly and non-quantitatively, and subclinical contralateral field defects, though common, do not predict conversion.

question: A patient with lung cancer of the right upper lobe has right upper eyelid ptosis and anisocoria that is greater in the dark with a right miotic pupil. What is the best definition of a positive cocaine test for unilateral Horner syndrome?

options.A: No dilation OD 30 minutes after instillation of two drops of cocaine 10% OD only
options.B: < 1 mm dilation OD 30 minutes after instillation of two drops of cocaine 10% OD only
options.C: Reversal of anisocoria 30 minutes after instillation of two drops of cocaine 10% OU
options.D: > 1 mm anisocoria 30 minutes after instillation of two drops of cocaine 10% OU

explanation: Drop testing to confirm the diagnosis of Horner syndrome is important in clinical practice and on standardized tests. Historically, the most commonly utilized drop test for the confirmation of Horner syndrome is cocaine testing. The response of a normal pupil to cocaine 10% is dilation because cocaine blocks reuptake of norepinephrine at the pre-synaptic cleft allowing more norepinephrine to function in stimulation of the pupillary dilator muscle. The response of a Horner syndrome pupil to cocaine is no or poor dilation because there is a shortage of norepinephrine in the synaptic cleft. Despite blockage of pre-synaptic norepinephrine reuptake by cocaine in a Horner syndrome eye, there is already limited norepinephrine in the synaptic cleft to cause dilation. The most accurate means to measure a positive response, therefore, is a relative comparison of dilation between the two eyes. If anisocoria is physiologic, for instance, both pupils will dilate equally (or nearly equally) leading to less than 1 mm anisocoria 30 minutes following instillation of cocaine 10% in both eyes. Of note, "reversal of anisocoria" indicates Horner syndrome following application of apraclonidine 1%. In other words, the Horner syndrome pupil will dilate much more than the normal pupil after instillation of apraclonidine. This phenomenon occurs since the Horner iris dilator muscle develops adrenergic supersensitivity. This fact is quite useful since apraclonidine is typically easier to obtain than cocaine in most eye clinics.

review.explanation: Cocaine 10% blocks reuptake of noradrenaline at the iris dilator, so a normally innervated pupil dilates while an oculosympathetically denervated Horner pupil does not, whatever the level of the lesion. Because the magnitude of a normal eye's response varies between individuals, the test is standardised by instilling drops in both eyes and comparing them, and a post-cocaine anisocoria of about 1 mm or more, with 0.8 mm often quoted, confirms Horner syndrome. Options A and B are wrong because instilling in one eye only removes the internal control, and absolute dilation of a single eye is not a reliable criterion. Reversal of anisocoria in option C is the endpoint of the apraclonidine test, which exploits denervation supersensitivity of the dilator, not the cocaine test.

question: What treatment for tuberculosis causes "orange-red" tears?
explanation: All of the rifamycins (e.g. rifampin, rifapentine, rifabutin) may cause orangered-orange discoloration of body fluids (including the tears) and also blepharoconjunctivitis. Both isoniazid and ethambutol may cause toxic optic neuropathy. A typical presentation of this toxic optic neuropathy is central visual field defects with loss of visual acuity and dyschromatopsia (especially for green). Typically, there is some visual improvement after cessation of the drug, but some visual field defects and loss of contrast sensitivity can persist. The incidence of ethambutol-related optic neuropathy after >2 months of use is approximately 18% in patients taking more than 35 mg/kg/day. The most clinically significant adverse effects of pyrazinamide are hepatotoxicity, gastrointestinal intolerance, polyarthralgias, and asymptomatic hyperuricemia. It can be argued that pyrazinamide also has ocular side effects in that patients can have icteric sclera from drug-induced hepatitis. However, the ocular side effects of isoniazid, ethambutol, and rifampin are much more characteristic and thus testable. You are performing cataract surgery for a 80-year-old woman with a dense "red"

review.explanation: Rifampin and the other rifamycins are excreted in body fluids and turn urine, sweat, saliva and tears orange-red, which is harmless but permanently stains soft contact lenses, so patients must be warned in advance. Isoniazid and ethambutol are the antituberculous drugs to fear ophthalmically because both cause toxic optic neuropathy, ethambutol classically dose- and duration-related with central scotomas, reduced acuity and red-green dyschromatopsia, requiring baseline and interval visual monitoring. Pyrazinamide causes hepatotoxicity, hyperuricaemia and polyarthralgia rather than any distinctive ocular sign.

This is because it is very easy for vitreous to occlude the small openings that are generally made for a laser peripheral iridotomy (LPI). According to the BCSC Glaucoma book, these surgical PIs should be placed at the 12 o'clock position in this situation. Surgical iridectomies should be performed at the 6 o'clock position (i.e. inferiorly) for patients undergoing endothelial keratoplasty (e.g. DSEK or DMEK) or having silicone oil left in the eye for retinal detachment repair. The reason being is that the injected air bubble or silicone oil bubble can float up and occlude a 12 o'clock iridectomy. (Editor's note: yes, we are aware of the 2014 AJO article from Ike Ahmed's group that concluded that temporal placement of a LPI was associated with less dysphotopsia compared to superior placement. However, the BCSC Glaucoma book explicitly states that a superior surgical PI should be performed during the time of ACIOL placement) Vera V, Naqi A, Belovay GW, Varma DK, Ahmed II. Dysphotopsia after temporal versus superior laser peripheral iridotomy: a prospective randomized paired eye trial. Am J Ophthalmol. 2014;157:929-35. review.explanation: Whenever an anterior chamber intraocular lens is placed, a patent iridectomy is required to prevent pupillary block, and it should be made surgically at the time of the operation, because a laser iridotomy in an eye that has just had vitreous prolapse is very likely to be plugged by residual vitreous strands. BCSC places this surgical iridectomy superiorly, at 12 o'clock, where it lies beneath the upper lid and is less likely to produce dysphotopsia. The inferior 6 o'clock position is reserved for eyes that will contain something buoyant, namely an air or gas bubble after endothelial keratoplasty or silicone oil after retinal detachment repair, because a bubble floats up and occludes a superior iridectomy. Option B is unsafe, and options C and D defer to a laser procedure that may well close.

question: 3+ conjunctival injection and a 20% hypopyon. There is no history of past ocular surgery or trauma. Dilated fundus exam shows a retinal vasculitis, macular edema, and significant vitreous cell. On review of systems, the patient complains of recurrent mouth pain and dysuria. Which of the following HLA-associations would this patient most likely have?
explanation: Individuals with Behcet's disease typically have more prominent non-ocular manifestations than ocular ones. Systemic manifestations include recurrent oral ulcers, epididymitis, skins lesions (e.g. erythema nodosum), CNS involvement, and arthritis. The anterior segment is usually more prominently involved in Behcet's disease and includes a severe uveitis often with hypopyon formation. Posterior segment signs include widespread occlusive vasculitis, retinal necrosis, ischemic optic neuropathy, and severe vitritis. This disease is associated with HLA-B51. HLA-A29 is associated with birdshot choroidopathy; HLA-DR2 is associated with pars planitis; and HLA-B27 is associated with the various spondylarthropathies (e.g. ankylosing spondylitis).

review.explanation: Recurrent oral ulceration, genital ulceration presenting as dysuria, a hypopyon uveitis with intense injection, and an occlusive retinal vasculitis with vitritis and macular oedema is Behcet disease, associated with HLA-B51 and classically prevalent along the historical Silk Road. The hypopyon of Behcet is characteristically mobile and shifts with head position, and the sight-threatening element is the posterior occlusive vasculitis, which requires systemic immunosuppression rather than corticosteroid alone. HLA-A29 is birdshot chorioretinopathy, HLA-DR2 or DR15 is linked to pars planitis, and HLA-B27 underlies the acute recurrent unilateral anterior uveitis of the spondyloarthropathies, which is the main mimic here because it too can form a hypopyon, but it does not produce retinal vasculitis or oral and genital ulceration.

question: A 27-year-old old man, who was recently started on systemic therapy for posterior uveitis secondary to tuberculosis, presents to the emergency room with a complaint of reddish colored urine, sweat and tears. Which of the following drugs is most likely causing these symptoms?
explanation: Rifampin, is an antibiotic used in the treatment of several types of bacterial infections, including tuberculosis, leprosy, and Legionnaire's disease. A common, but harmless, side effect of rifampin is the red/orange coloration of urine, sweat, saliva, or tears. Though this coloration is harmless, soft contact lenses may be permanently stained.

review.explanation: Rifampin colours urine, sweat, saliva and tears orange-red because the drug and its metabolites are excreted in body fluids, and the reaction is harmless, needing only reassurance and a warning about permanent staining of soft contact lenses. Streptomycin causes vestibulocochlear toxicity and nephrotoxicity, ethambutol causes a dose-related toxic optic neuropathy with reduced acuity and dyschromatopsia, and pyrazinamide causes hepatotoxicity and hyperuricaemia. None of the other three discolours secretions, so the history alone identifies the drug.

question: A scenario about pars planitis asking about the content of snow banking?
explanation: Histologic studies show condensed vitreous, fibroblasts, lymphocytes, and lymphocyte cuffing of the peripheral retinal veins. Snowbanks and snowballs consist of a fibrovascular layer containing mononuclear leukocytes and fibrocyte-like cells, as well as vitreous collagen, Muller cells and fibrous astrocytes. https://eyewiki.aao.org/Intermediate_Uveitis

review.explanation: The snowbank of pars planitis is an organised fibrovascular and fibroglial membrane overlying the pars plana and peripheral retina, containing new vessels, condensed vitreous collagen, fibrous astrocytes and Muller cell processes with scattered mononuclear leucocytes. Its vascularity matters clinically because it explains why these eyes can develop vitreous haemorrhage and tractional detachment, particularly in children. Multinucleated giant cells are the hallmark of granulomatous inflammation such as sarcoidosis and are not what constitutes a snowbank, so B is wrong. Macular oedema is the commonest cause of vision loss in pars planitis but is a separate finding, not the content of the snowbank.

question: 30 y/o African american patient with hilar lymphadenopathy, presented with acute eye pain and photophobia. What is the content of the finding that is depicted in the photo?
explanation: Similar Q from ophthaQ: The photograph depicts "mutton-fat" keratic precipitates (KP). In general, KP are simply deposits of inflammatory cells on the corneal endothelium. The shape of KP depends on its composition. For example, mutton-fat KP are larger since they are comprised of macrophages. "Small dot" KP are usually composed of fibrin while "punctate" KP are formed from neutrophils and lymphocytes.

review.explanation: The photograph shows large, greasy, mutton-fat keratic precipitates on the inferior corneal endothelium, the granulomatous pattern expected in a young Black patient with hilar lymphadenopathy and therefore sarcoidosis. Mutton-fat precipitates are large precisely because they consist of bulky mononuclear phagocytes, that is macrophages and the epithelioid cells they differentiate into, sometimes with multinucleated giant cells. Non-granulomatous precipitates are small and fine and are composed of lymphocytes and neutrophils, which is why lymphocytes and PMNs are wrong, and fine fibrin deposits give the small dot precipitates seen in HLA-B27 disease.
review.concern: Options A and C are not truly separable, since epithelioid cells are transformed macrophages and standard texts describe mutton-fat KPs as containing both. The item would be sound only if one of them were removed; macrophages is the choice usually keyed, so the source answer is defensible.

The glial component comprises vitreous collagen and fibrous astrocytes, whereas lymphocytic infiltrates are composed mainly of T helper cells. Reference: Yanoff & Duker 5th edition: - Histopathological studies of the snowbanks show glial and vascular proliferation,

review.explanation: Histopathology of the snowbank shows a fibrovascular and fibroglial membrane: proliferating glial tissue with fibrous astrocytes and condensed vitreous collagen, together with new blood vessels, and lymphocytic cuffing of the adjacent peripheral retinal veins with a predominance of T helper cells. The fibrovascular component is the answer because it accounts for the risk of vitreous haemorrhage and traction in these eyes. Lipid exudate would point to Coats disease or another exudative retinopathy, and accumulation of epithelioid histiocytes describes granuloma formation, which would suggest sarcoidosis rather than idiopathic pars planitis.

review.explanation: Elevated intraocular pressure during active anterior uveitis is the finding that should make you think of herpetic disease, because herpesviruses cause a trabeculitis that raises pressure at a time when most other uveitides lower it through ciliary body hyposecretion; pressures of 40 to 60 mm Hg are described, and inflammatory cells add further outflow obstruction. The supporting features of herpetic anterior uveitis are unilaterality, sectoral or patchy iris atrophy with a distorted pupil, reduced corneal sensation, and past or concurrent keratitis, and treatment requires antiviral cover alongside steroid. Stellate keratic precipitates do occur in herpetic and especially CMV anterior uveitis, but they are equally or more characteristic of Fuchs heterochromic uveitis, so they are the weaker discriminator here.
review.concern: I would answer B. BCSC Uveitis states that ocular hypertension associated with herpetic uveitis may be a helpful diagnostic hallmark, and in the same passage that diffuse or stellate KPs are not pathognomonic of any particular condition. The source explanation quotes both of those sentences yet keys A, so the explanation argues against its own answer. Raised IOP from trabeculitis is the classic teaching point for herpetic anterior uveitis, while stellate KPs are most strongly linked to Fuchs heterochromic uveitis and CMV anterior uveitis. This looks like a transcription error in the answer key rather than a genuine difference of opinion.

question: She states she has a history of glaucoma and has been on the same eyedrop for the past "many many years." She is unhappy with her previous eyecare provider because he ignores her when she says that her eyes are "all itchy and red from the eyedrops." Which of the following glaucoma medications is associated with the highest rate of this patient's reported side effects?
explanation: The brand name of apraclonidine is Iopidine. Of the choices listed, apraclonidine is associated with the highest incidence (~40%) of periocular blepharitis/dermatitis. The high incidence of this side effect limits apraclonidine's usefulness as chronic therapy for glaucoma. Today, its use is typically limited to prophylaxis against intraocular pressure spikes after laser and cataract surgeries. It is also used as an alternative agent to cocaine in the diagnosis of Horner's syndrome. It finds this use since apraclonidine has very weak alpha-1 agonist action and will not typically dilate a normal pupil. However, apraclonidine will dilate a Horner's pupil since the iris dilator develops adrenergic supersensitivity in this condition. Thus, "reversal of anisocoria" occurs when apraclonidine is instilled in the eye with Horner's syndrome. Other selective alpha-2 agonist eyedrops have a much lower incidence of ocular allergy According to the BCSC: Brimonidine tartrate 0.2% (preserved with benzalkonium chloride) (brand: Alphagan) -- 15% incidence Brimonidine tartrate 0.1% (preserved with Purite) (brand: Alphagan P) -<10% incidence

review.explanation: Apraclonidine causes allergic follicular conjunctivitis and periocular contact dermatitis in roughly 20 to 40 percent of patients on chronic therapy, by far the highest rate among the drugs listed, and that is exactly why its use is now confined to short-term blunting of pressure spikes around laser and cataract surgery. Brimonidine, a more selective alpha-2 agonist, causes the same reaction considerably less often and later, and less still with the purite-preserved lower concentrations. Dorzolamide typically causes stinging and a bitter taste, with sulfonamide hypersensitivity as its important allergy, and latanoprost causes conjunctival hyperaemia, lash growth and iris and periocular pigmentation rather than the itchy allergic dermatitis described.

question: a 45-year-old man presents with acute pain in the left eye. His intraocular pressure is 50 mmHg OS and slit-lamp exam finds a shallow anterior chamber with a subluxed lens that appears to be occluding the pupil. Which of the following office procedures is most appropriate for this patient?

options.A: two laser peripheral iridotomies 180 degrees apart from each other
options.B: two laser peripheral iridotomies 90 degrees away from each other
options.C: one laser peripheral iridotomy located at 12 o'clock
options.D: one laser peripheral iridotomy located at 6 o'clock

explanation: This patient presents with a displaced lens (i.e. "ectopia lentis") that is occluding the pupil and causing pupillary block glaucoma. According to the BCSC Glaucoma book, the definitive treatment would be cataract extraction, but two laser peripheral iridotomies situated 180 degrees apart from each other is the office procedure of choice to relieve the pupillary block. The presumptive reason why two LPIs would be ideal is because the ectopic lens could theoretically move and occlude one of the LPIs, but unlikely would be able to cover both simultaneously. Thus, pupillary block would be relieved by at least one of the patent LPIs. Ectopia lentis can also predispose to chronic angle closure glaucoma if peripheral anterior synechiae forms after repeated intermittent attacks of acute angle closure. (Editor's Note: you can find this tidbit about LPIs 180 degrees apart from each other under the "Angle-Closure Glaucoma" chapter in the BCSC Glaucoma book). A 45-year-old patient presents to your office with a 1-week history of idiopathic uveitis

review.explanation: A subluxed lens plugging the pupil produces pupillary block, and the office treatment is laser iridotomy, but in ectopia lentis BCSC recommends two iridotomies placed 180 degrees apart, because a mobile lens can shift and occlude a single opening whereas it cannot cover two diametrically opposed openings simultaneously. Placing them only 90 degrees apart leaves both within reach of the same displaced lens. A single iridotomy, superior or inferior, is the standard for ordinary phakic pupillary block but is unreliable when the blocking element is mobile. Definitive management once the acute block is broken is lens extraction.

question: in the right eye. He is currently taking prednisolone acetate 1% OD qid. His original level of anterior chamber inflammation was graded as 3+ and his IP was 33 mmHg. On his follow-up exam today, his intraocular pressure (IP) is 28 mmHg and there is 2+ cell in the anterior chamber in his right eye. Which of the following is the most appropriate management choice?

options.A: decrease PF to adaily: start timolol 0.5% bid
options.B: decrease PF to qdaily; start latanoprost qhs
options.C: increase PF to q2 hours; start pilocarpine 1% bid
options.D: increase PF to q2 hours; start brimonidine bid

explanation: This patient's elevated IOP is not likely the result of a corticosteroid-response since he has only been taking them for 1 week. The more likely cause of this elevated IOP is inadequate suppression of inflammation; therefore, his topical corticosteroids should be increased to eliminate this residual inflammation. Prostaglandin-analogs and miotics (i.e. pilocarpine) should probably be avoided in cases of active inflammation due to reports of them exacerbating inflammation and/or causing cystoid macular edema. a 78-year-old woman with a history of poor vision in the right eye for "a long time"

review.explanation: After only one week of prednisolone this pressure rise is almost certainly not a steroid response, which typically takes two to six weeks, and the persisting 2+ cell tells you the inflammation is undertreated and that the trabecular meshwork is obstructed by inflammatory cells and debris. The correct move is therefore to intensify rather than reduce the corticosteroid and to add a pressure-lowering agent, and brimonidine is a good choice because it lowers pressure without any pro-inflammatory effect. Prostaglandin analogues are relatively contraindicated in active uveitis because of concern about worsening inflammation and cystoid macular oedema, excluding B, and pilocarpine is contraindicated because it increases vascular permeability and promotes posterior synechiae, excluding C. Options A and B are additionally wrong because they taper steroid while inflammation is still active.

question: presents to your clinic complaining of severe pain in the right eye for the past 2 days. Slit-lamp photograph of this eye is shown above. Of note, there was 2+ cell/flare but no keratic precipitates. The anterior chamber depth is grade III by the Shaffer system. Intraocular pressure of this eye is 48 mmHg. Which of the following is the MOST LIKELY cause of her symptoms? a 78-year-old woman
explanation: Phacolytic glaucoma is one of the 4 lens-induced glaucomas. The other three are phacomorphic glaucoma, lens particle glaucoma, and phacoantigenic glaucoma. Phacolytic glaucoma occurs in the presence of a mature or hypermature cataract. In these cataracts, there is an increased concentration of high molecular weight lens protein. These proteins are released through microscopic openings in the lens capsule (i.e. not trauma/surgery induced) and clog up the trabecular meshwork. In addition, macrophages (i.e. the "refractile bodies") phagocytize these large proteins and also clog up the trabecular meshwork. This combination of factors leads to an acute rise in intraocular pressure. The BCSC states that some of distinguishing features of phacolytic glaucoma are: lack of keratic precipitates(which are found in phacoantigenic glaucoma), an open angle (contrast this with the closed angle in phacomorphic glaucoma), and a macroscopically-intact lens capsule (contrast this with lensparticle glaucoma which often involves a violated lens capsule). Phacoanaphylactic uveitis (also known as phacoantigenic uveitis) occurs when the capsular bag is violated which leads to inflammation. Phacomorphic glaucoma occurs when the lens becomes so large that it pushes the iris forward and closes the angle. The treatment is surgical removal of the lens. Both phacolytic and phacoantigenic glaucomas can present with a hot eye that contains a hypermature cataract. However, lack of keratic precipitates is more characteristic of phacolytic glaucoma. Cytology of aqueous would reveal lens-laden macrophages in phacolytic glaucoma. Phacomorphic glaucoma would present with a shallow anterior chamber while lens particle glaucoma would present with MACROscopic lens pieces in the anterior chamber (in contrast to MICROscopic lens proteins as in phacolytic glaucoma). (Image credit: Cogan Pathology Collection found at: http://cogancollection.nei.nih.gov

review.explanation: An elderly eye with a hypermature cataract, an acutely painful pressure of 48 mm Hg, marked cell and flare but no keratic precipitates, and a widely open angle at Shaffer grade III, is phacolytic glaucoma: high-molecular-weight lens protein leaks through an intact but microscopically permeable capsule and, with the swollen macrophages that engulf it, obstructs an anatomically open trabecular meshwork. Phacomorphic glaucoma is excluded by the open angle, since it is an angle closure driven by an intumescent lens. Lens particle glaucoma requires a capsular breach from trauma or surgery, which is absent. Phacoantigenic glaucoma is a granulomatous reaction to lens protein after capsular disruption and characteristically shows keratic precipitates, which the stem specifically says are absent. Definitive treatment is cataract extraction once the pressure is medically controlled.

explanation: A cyclodialysis cleft represents a disinsertion of the ciliary body from the scleral spur, allowing flow of aqueous humor from the anterior segment into the suprachoroidal space. Cyclodialysis clefts generally occur in three clinical settings: 1) as a surgical complication,

review.explanation: A cyclodialysis cleft is a disinsertion of the ciliary body from the scleral spur and is a classic sequel of blunt trauma with hyphaema; the direct route it creates from anterior chamber into the suprachoroidal space, combined with reduced aqueous production, produces prolonged profound hypotony such as the pressure of 4 mm Hg described. The diagnostically decisive event is spontaneous closure of the cleft, which abruptly restores aqueous production against an outflow system that has been suppressed and is often also damaged, causing a sudden marked pressure spike with pain and headache. Angle recession glaucoma does raise pressure after trauma, but it does so insidiously months to years later and does not explain the preceding months of hypotony. Gonioscopy or ultrasound biomicroscopy confirms the cleft.

explanation: Patients who have spasm of the near reflex present with excessive convergence, accommodation, and miosis. These patients have normal ductions (e.g. one eye covered), but an abduction deficit on version eye movements (i.e. when both eyes open). Spasm of the near reflex is also known as "ciliary spasm" or "convergence spasm." The cause of this acquired, non-accommodative esotropia is thought to be functional (e.g. related to stress and anxiety). These patients present with acute esotropia that alternates with being orthotropic. They often have myopia on manifest, but if cyclopleged, have no significant myopia or no additional myopia beyond their baseline refraction. The treatment of spasm of the near reflex includes: Identifying and addressing causative factors (e.g. emotional stress/anxiety); Cycloplegic agents (e.g. atropine); Hyperopic correction (if patient is significantly hyperopic); Bifocals (to help with the excessive accommodation); Rarely: botulinum injections of the medial rectus muscles and/or strabismus surgery (only if the spasm cannot be broken)

explanation: Traumatic optic neuropathy can be divided into two subtypes according to mechanism of injury: Direct (DTON), which is due to direct injury to the optic nerve itself, such as laceration, stretch, compression, or impingement. The mechanism of injury results in physical disruption of the nerve. For example: Orbital apex fractures, bone fragments impinging the optic canal, large retrobulbar hematoma, or robust optic nerve edema causing it to suffer a compressive "compartment syndrome" effect within the confines of the optic canal. In some cases, if a direct ongoing cause of nerve injury can be identified, it may be addressed with surgical intervention (e.g. optic nerve decompression). Indirect (ITON), which occurs from an injury/impact remote from the optic nerve. It is thought that the shock waves transmitted through the orbital bones and soft tissues are responsible for causing this type of neuropathy, although the exact mechanism is not well understood. The bottom line is that nothing directly crushed, stretched, compressed, or cut the nerve itself. This question describes a case of ITON. The patient has normal nerve appearance on dilated fundus exam and CT imaging, without an apparent ongoing insult to the optic nerve. Unfortunately there are no good evidence- based surgical or medical options that have been shown to help with ITON. Notable reports and research studies: Anderson RL et al described a scenario of blindness following blunt head trauma (PubMed link). The International Optic Nerve Trauma Study (IONTS), which was a nonrandomized study that evaluated megadose steroids (n=85), optic nerve decompression (n=33), or observation (n=9) for the treatment of traumatic optic neuropathy within 1 week of the event. The study showed that observation was non-inferiorto either medical or surgical treatment. However, the study struggled with recruitment of enough patients, so the conclusions were limited by small sample size (PubMed link). Corticosteroid Randomisation after Significant Head Injury (CRASH) study was a large randomized controlled trial of the efficacy and safety of systemic steroids in patients with acute traumatic brain injury. The risk of death was significantly higher in the steroid group (25.7%) than the placebo group (22.3%). The risk of severe disability was also higher in the steroid group. High-dose steroids are contraindicated in patients with neuro-trauma. The NASCIS trial showed possible improvement in recovery after spinal cord injuries in patients treated with high-dose systemic steroids initiated within 8 hours after injury. The study had several limitations. A good summary of NASCIS and of several other studies related to traumatic optic neuropathy is available [here]. In summary, there is unfortunately no strong, congruent evidence base for intervention in ITON. High-dose steroids raise the risk of death or severe impairment if there is a brain injury present. Optic nerve decompression carries risks of complications from surgery, with the potential to directly injure the optic nerve. Decompression may be beneficial in some cases of DTON, but requires a careful conversation with the patient about its risks. A transorbital or trans-ethmoidal approach, or an endoscopic trans-sphenoidal approach (often by ENT) can be used to decompress the optic canal in these cases. a 67-year-old woman falls down a flight of stairs and is brought into the trauma bay. She has multiple injuries including panfacial fractures and her CT is shown above. The trauma team calls you because her right eye is proptotic and the lids are "tight." When you arrive, you see the linear density in the inferolateral quadrant of the orbit

review.explanation: This is indirect traumatic optic neuropathy: a dense afferent defect after a frontal impact, with a normal fundus and a CT showing an intact canal, no fragments, no haematoma and a nerve of normal calibre and enhancement. The International Optic Nerve Trauma Study found no benefit of either corticosteroids or optic canal decompression over observation, so neither surgical option is justified when no compressive lesion is demonstrable. Megadose steroids are worse than merely unhelpful here because the patient has a frontal lobe contusion, and the CRASH trial showed increased mortality with high-dose steroids in acute head injury. Decompression, whether transethmoidal or endoscopic, is reserved for an identifiable ongoing compressive cause such as an impinging bone fragment or an optic nerve sheath haematoma.

The globe has subconjunctival hemorrhage 360 degrees but the pupil is round and there are no signs of a ruptured globe. You decide to perform a canthotomy and inferior cantholysis. After successfully doing so, you check the pressure again and it is 44mmHg. What is the next best step?

options.B: Start Diamox and check the pressure in an hour

explanation: Orbital compartment syndrome is defined by an acute rise in orbital tension and needs to be recognized and treated promptly to avoid permanent visual loss. If you know the mechanism of injury in this case is a retrobulbar hemorrhage, you must act to lower the pressure with mechanical factors first rather than medical ones (i.e. this is a different entity of increase intraocular pressure as compared to an IOP-spike a day after cataract surgery). The best first step is to perform a canthotomy with a complete inferior cantholysis. After successfully doing so, if the pressure has not returned to below 30-35 mmHg or so, then you probably have more to do. While it is certainly one option to try topical or systemic medical therapy, or even consider a paracentesis, the best option is to proceed with lysing the superior crus of the lateral canthal tendon to allow for further prolapse of the orbital contents forward to relieve the orbital tension.

review.explanation: Orbital compartment syndrome from retrobulbar haemorrhage is a mechanical problem and demands a mechanical solution, delivered within minutes because the optic nerve and posterior ciliary circulation tolerate very little ischaemic time. If the pressure remains above roughly 30-35 mmHg and the lids are still tight after canthotomy and inferior cantholysis, the release is incomplete, and lysing the superior crus of the lateral canthal tendon frees the lid from the rim and allows further anterior prolapse of orbital contents. Brimonidine and acetazolamide act on aqueous dynamics, are far too slow, and do nothing about retrobulbar pressure. Paracentesis lowers intraocular pressure while leaving orbital pressure and optic nerve perfusion unchanged, and adds the risks of an intraocular procedure in a traumatised eye.

question: What creates the upper eyelid crease?

options.B: Contour of the tarsus visible through skin
options.C: Embryologic fusion of eyelid tissue to brow tissue
options.D: Levator attachments to orbicularis and skin

explanation: Just superior to the tarsus, the levator splits into two portions. One portion has fine fibrous projections that attach to the orbicularis and skin. These fibers help anchor the skin and orbicularis onto the levator aponeurosis, forming the eyelid crease. The fold of tissue that you often see superior to the crease is created by an overhang of skin, orbicularis, and sometimes prolapsed orbital fat. Clinical correlate: This anatomy explains why patients with aponeurotic (involutional) ptosis often have a higher eyelid crease on the ptotic lid. When the levator aponeurosis dehisces from its tarsal attachments and slips backward (supero-posterior), the attachments forming the crease are displaced superiorly as well. An example of this is shown in the photo

review.explanation: Just above the tarsus the levator aponeurosis sends fine fibrous slips anteriorly that insert into the pretarsal orbicularis and overlying skin; when the levator contracts these slips pull the skin inward and create the eyelid crease. This explains why Asian eyelids, in which the orbital septum fuses low and preaponeurotic fat descends to block these attachments, have a low crease or none at all. It also explains the clinical sign of aponeurotic ptosis, where dehiscence of the aponeurosis from the tarsus lets the whole complex slide superiorly and raises the crease on the ptotic side. The tarsus itself is not visible through skin, the canthal tendons anchor the lids horizontally rather than creating a horizontal crease line, and there is no embryologic brow-to-lid fusion event responsible for it.

question: All of the following are good reasons to perform an evisceration over an enucleation EXCEPT:

options.D: patient unable to undergo general anesthesia

explanation: Patients with suspicion of intraocular malignancies should undergo enucleation. Some authors recommend against evisceration to guard against the risk of removing an occult malignancy which could be spread along tissue layers. However, evisceration is often performed and is often a slightly faster procedure than enucleation. Therefore, it is a good option for patients who cannot have a long procedure or general anesthesia. Additionally, it is a good option for a patient with endophthalmitis and poor visual potential to prevent possible spread along the meninges. Lastly, evisceration involves removing the contents of the eye and, if a prosthetic implant is placed into the residual scleral bed, can usually result in better movement of the prosthetic since the extraocular muscles are still attached to the globe.

review.explanation: Any suspicion of intraocular malignancy is a contraindication to evisceration, because the procedure disrupts the tumour, leaves sclera behind, precludes proper pathologic staging of extrascleral extension, and risks orbital seeding; enucleation with an intact globe is required. The other three are genuine advantages of evisceration: it is quicker and can be done under local or block anaesthesia in a patient who cannot tolerate general anaesthesia, it preserves the muscle attachments to the scleral shell so prosthetic motility is generally better, and in endophthalmitis it avoids opening the subarachnoid space along the optic nerve. Note that evisceration also carries a theoretical risk of sympathetic ophthalmia, though the actual incidence is very low.

question: you performed an enucleation on a patient on Thursday. On Friday, your patient looks good with the conformer fully in place. On Saturday, you receive a call from your patient who states that the conformer fell out of his eye and he cannot get it back in himself. You are not scheduled to see him for one month. Which of the following is the most appropriate response to this patient?

options.A: "I'll see you next week and will put the conformer back in for you."
options.B: "Just leave it out until I see you in a month."
options.C: "Meet me at the office today and I'll put it back in."
options.D: "It does not matter if it the conformer stays in or not. It is just there for comfort."

explanation: After the enucleation, an acrylic or silicone conformer is placed in the conjunctival fornices to maintain the conjunctival space that will eventually hold the prosthesis. The conformer helps prevent cicatrization of the fornices. Left without a conformer for several days, the fornices can adhere to each other and make placing a prosthetic very difficult in the future. Mucous membrane grafting to reconstruct the fornices may be needed in such instances. To avoid this situation, conformers (and also prostheses) "should not be removed for periods greater than 24 hours" (verbatim from the BCSC Oculoplastics book). Editor's Note: so if you are a 1st year resident taking this call from the patient, just go in and put the conformer back in for the patient!

review.explanation: The conformer maintains the conjunctival fornices in the early postoperative period, and if it is left out the raw conjunctival surfaces adhere to one another and the fornices contract, sometimes irreversibly within days. Standard oculoplastic teaching is that a conformer or prosthesis should not be left out for more than 24 hours, so the patient must be seen the same day and it must be replaced. Waiting a week or a month risks fornix cicatrisation that later requires mucous membrane grafting to rebuild a socket capable of holding a prosthesis. Telling the patient the conformer is only for comfort is factually wrong; comfort is incidental to its structural role.

question: A 71-year-old man presents with concerns about a mass which appeared about 6 months ago, and has slowly enlarged to the point that it now protrudes between his lids. As shown in the photo, exam finds a glistening yellow mass which is painless, soft, and mobile beneath the conjunctiva. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This newly-developed, soft, glistening, yellow, mobile sub-conjunctival mass is prolapsed orbital fat. In contrast, lipodermoid (aka dermolipoma) (choice "A") is a congenital choristoma comprised of dense fibroconnective tissue and fat, which would have been present since birth, rather than appearing at age 71. Lipodermoids are occasionally associated with oculoauriculovertebral dysplasia (i.e. Goldenhar syndrome). Hemangiopericytoma (choice "B") would be a firm mass, usually located in the retrobulbar intraconal space. Pleomorphic adenoma (choice "D") of the orbit forms a firm mass arising from the lacrimal gland, often causing the appearance of superotemporal lid fullness or non-axial proptosis rather than a sub-conjunctival mass. A 76-year-old woman underwent bilateral upper eyelid blepharoplasty. She is a

review.explanation: A soft, mobile, glistening yellow subconjunctival mass that appeared recently in an elderly patient and slowly enlarged is prolapsed orbital fat, which herniates forward through an attenuated Tenon capsule and orbital septum with age, most often superotemporally. A lipodermoid looks similar but is a congenital choristoma present from birth, typically fixed at the lateral canthal region and sometimes associated with Goldenhar syndrome, so a lesion first noted at age 71 excludes it. Hemangiopericytoma, now classified as a solitary fibrous tumour, is a firm intraconal mass presenting with proptosis rather than a subconjunctival lump. Pleomorphic adenoma arises in the lacrimal gland and produces a firm superotemporal mass with slowly progressive non-axial proptosis and globe displacement, not a soft mobile conjunctival mass.

She had been doing well at her follow-up appointment on post-operative day #5, with all incisions clean, dry, and intact. explanation: The photo shows a partially-dehisced upper lid blepharoplasty incision. The dehisced area is healing by secondary intention. The golden-brown area along the central incision is dried serosanguinous drainage covering the granulation tissue which has formed in the exposed wound bed. Wound dehiscence after blepharoplasty surgery occurs in approximately 2% of patients, usually only involving a short segment of the incision. A small dehiscence can be allowed to heal by secondary intention. A larger dehiscence should be prepped sterile, numbed with local anesthetic, debrided to remove granulation tissue and freshen the wound edges, then sutured closed. Optimal control of diabetes perioperatively helps improve wound healing, thereby decreasing the risk of dehiscence. Anything that impairs wound healing will increase the risk of wound dehiscence, including obesity (choice "C"), poor nutrition, diabetes, smoking, or alcohol intake (choice "D"). Significant bleeding beneath the incision can create tension on the wound which can lead to dehiscence (choice "A"). Guo S, DiPietro LA. Factors affecting wound healing. J Dent Res. 2010;89:219-29. Kashkouli MB, et al. Upper blepharoplasty and lateral wound dehiscence. Middle E Afr J

review.explanation: The picture is a partially dehisced upper lid blepharoplasty incision at day 10 healing by secondary intention, and among the listed variables the only modifiable one that impairs wound healing in this patient is her diabetes. Hyperglycaemia impairs neutrophil function, collagen deposition and fibroblast proliferation, so tighter perioperative glycaemic control genuinely reduces dehiscence risk. Continued anticoagulation would raise the risk of haematoma and would not have prevented dehiscence; her BMI of 23 is normal and a higher BMI impairs rather than improves healing; and alcohol impairs wound healing and increases bleeding risk, so nightly wine is not protective. Management of a small dehiscence is conservative, while a longer one is debrided, freshened and resutured.

question: A 60-year old male with no past ocular history undergoes a 6-hour cardiac bypass surgery. When he awakes from surgery he is found to have hand motion vision in both eyes. Aside from his abnormal vision, sluggish pupillary function, and pupillary light-near dissociation, his exam is unremarkable (including his dilated fundus exam). What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Posterior ischemic optic neuropathy (PION) is much rarer than anterior ischemic optic neuropathy but similarly is believed to be related to hypoperfusion of the posterior optic nerve. Usually the hypoperfusion is due to a perfect storm of contributing risk factors including anemia, hypotension, poor cardiac output, hypovolemia, and cardiopulmonary instability during surgery. Rarely PION can be related to a vasculitic process including giant cell arteritis, lupus-associated vasculitis, polyarteritis nodosa, and VZV related vasculitis. Unlike anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, PION almost always has a normal appearing optic nerve in the acute phase. Dorsal midbrain syndrome does include pupillary light-near dissociation, but has other findings not exhibited in this patient and does not typically result in sudden bilateral vision loss. As an aside, any disease process causing bilateral optic neuropathy can result in pupillary light-near dissociation. A 20-year-old female complains of intermittent binocular diplopia when she is reading late at night. Review of old photographs reveals a chronic right head tilt since early

review.explanation: Bilateral severe vision loss discovered on waking from prolonged cardiac or spine surgery, with sluggish pupils, light-near dissociation and completely normal optic discs, is the classic picture of perioperative posterior ischaemic optic neuropathy. The infarct is retrobulbar, so the disc appears normal acutely and becomes pale only after four to eight weeks; the risk factors are prolonged surgery, hypotension, anaemia, large fluid shifts and venous congestion. Both forms of anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy are excluded by the normal fundus examination, since by definition they present with a swollen disc. Dorsal midbrain syndrome does cause light-near dissociation but comes with upgaze palsy, convergence-retraction nystagmus and lid retraction, and it does not cause bilateral hand-motion vision with a normal afferent pathway examination.

question: childhood. Alignment testing shows a left hypertropia that is worse on downgaze and right gaze. When testing each eye individually, eye movements appear full. When testing eye movements under binocular conditions there is a prominent up shoot of the left eye on far right gaze. Which of the following accurately describes her eye movement examination?
explanation: A good careful motility examination includes both ductions testing and versions testing Ductions describe testing of ocular motility under monocular conditions (in other words, covering one eye and testing the other eye) while versions are tested under binocular conditions (both eyes open). Why does it matter? Sometimes, as in this case, a subtle motility deficit may not be appreciated under monocular ductions testing but is obvious when testing versions. In this case, the patient suffers from a classic case of a left congenital 4th nerve palsy with overaction of the inferior oblique. The inferior oblique "overaction" is a result of a weak antagonistic superior oblique muscle. The inferior oblique overaction effect is always most evident in adduction where the muscle has its greatest elevation effect.

review.explanation: Ductions are monocular movements tested with the fellow eye covered, whereas versions are binocular conjugate movements; the stem states that each eye moves fully alone but that the left eye overelevates in right gaze when both eyes are open, which is by definition normal ductions with abnormal versions. The pattern of a left hypertropia worse in right gaze and downgaze with an upshoot of the left eye in adduction is a congenital left fourth nerve palsy with secondary inferior oblique overaction, and inferior oblique overaction is characteristically seen only under binocular versions. This is exactly why a complete motility examination must include both, since a purely monocular examination would have called this eye normal. Completing the assessment with Parks three-step testing and looking for a head tilt and facial asymmetry confirms the diagnosis.

question: What will differentiate between lesion in cavernous sinus and lesion in orbital apex?
explanation: Orbital apex syndrome (OAS) involves cranial neuropathies in association with optic nerve dysfunction. Orbital apex syndrome is symptomatically related to superior orbital fissure syndrome and cavernous sinus syndrome with similar etiologies. The distinction is the precise anatomic involvement of the disease process. Signs/Symptoms: The most common initial manifestation of OAS is visual loss and ophthalmoplegia involving multiple cranial nerves Visual loss is due to CNII involvement. Optic disc edema or subsequent optic atrophy may develop within weeks to months. Ophthalmoplegia with variable diplopia, mydriasis, and ptosis due to CNIII, IV, VI involvement Absence of corneal sensations and corneal reflex Pupillary abnormalities: Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD) Choroidal folds Periorbital/facial pain and hypoesthesia of the forehead due to CNV involvement. Proptosis with or without orbital congestion Chemosis and/or conjunctival injection Cavernous Sinus Syndrome (CSS): Cavernous sinus syndrome may also present with multiple oculomotor cranial neuropathies, including III, IV, VI, and sensory dysfunction from involvement of V1. The internal carotid artery may also be involved with the primary process in CSS. Optic nerve dysfunction should not occur in CSS.

review.explanation: The optic nerve is the discriminator: it runs through the orbital apex within the annulus of Zinn but never enters the cavernous sinus, so visual loss with a relative afferent pupillary defect localises the lesion to the apex rather than to the sinus. Cranial nerves III, IV, VI and V1 traverse both regions and their involvement therefore cannot separate the two. The nasociliary nerve is a V1 branch present at the apex but its parent trunk is already in the cavernous sinus, so it is not discriminating either. Oculosympathetic fibres travel with the internal carotid through the cavernous sinus and then join V1, so a Horner syndrome plus a sixth nerve palsy actually points to the cavernous sinus, but sympathetic involvement alone is not the cleanest separator.

PION is characterized clinically by acute, painless vision loss in one or both eyes, the presence of a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) in unilateral or bilateral but asymmetric cases and a normal fundus (retrobulbar optic neuropathy). - PION is distinguished from AION by the appearance of a typically normal optic nerve head in PION compared with a swollen optic disc in AION. - For perioperative PION, in which bilateral disease is common, a relative afferent pupil defect may not be detected unless the damage is asymmetric (10), but the poor pupil reaction to light in both eyes results in a light-near dissociation, with greater pupil contraction to an attempted near effort compared to the pupil response to bright light https://webeye.ophth.uiowa.edu/eyeforum/cases/212-PION.htm

review.explanation: This is the same perioperative scenario as the earlier question: prolonged surgery, bilateral profound vision loss on waking, and a normal anterior and posterior segment examination, which means the optic nerve injury is retrobulbar and therefore posterior ischaemic optic neuropathy. Poor light reactivity in both eyes with better constriction to near effort produces the light-near dissociation described, and a relative afferent pupillary defect may be absent precisely because the damage is symmetric. Anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy is excluded by the normal-looking discs, since disc oedema is required for that diagnosis. Dorsal midbrain syndrome causes light-near dissociation but with supranuclear upgaze palsy and convergence-retraction nystagmus, and it does not cause bilateral counting-fingers acuity.

review.explanation: Loss of vision means optic nerve involvement, and ptosis means third nerve involvement, so the lesion must be at a site where both structures lie together, which is the orbital apex. At the apex the optic nerve enters via the optic canal alongside the annulus of Zinn through which III, VI, and the nasociliary branch of V1 pass, so orbital apex syndrome combines visual loss with ophthalmoplegia, ptosis, a fixed pupil and V1 sensory loss. A brainstem lesion could produce a third nerve palsy with ptosis, but visual loss would then require a separate lesion, since the optic nerve is not in the brainstem. Typical causes at the apex include invasive fungal sinusitis, tumour, granulomatous inflammation and trauma, so urgent contrast orbital imaging is indicated.

question: Hallucinations and illusions are related but clearly distinct subjective visual phenomena with differing etiologies. Which of the following is associated with hallucinations as opposed to illusions?
explanation: Illusions are an optical or cortical distortion of an object seen in reality. Metamorphopsia describes an abnormal subjective curvature or waviness to objects that in reality are straight. It usually occurs as a result of macular disease such as macular degeneration or epiretinal membrane. The Pulfrich phenomenon is the illusion that an object moving perpendicular to a person's line of sight is actually moving toward them or away from them. Theoretically, it could be seen in any disease affecting the conduction of visual information in one optic nerve more than the other. It is usually described in patients who have partially recovered following a bout of optic neuritis. Micropsia is the illusion that objects appear smaller than they should and is indicative of macular pathology, parietal lobe pathology, or an unusual migraine headache related phenomenon known as the "Alice in Wonderland" effect. Photopsias associated with cancer associated retinopathy, MEWDS, AZOOR, birdshot chorioretinopathy, and PVD are all simple, unformed hallucinations because they do not arise from distortion of an object in reality.

review.explanation: A hallucination is a visual percept generated without any external stimulus, whereas an illusion is a distortion of something genuinely present. Photopsias, flashes of light with no light source, are therefore hallucinations, whether they arise from vitreoretinal traction, retinal disease or occipital cortical irritation. Metamorphopsia and micropsia are distortions of the size and shape of real objects and are illusions, typically from macular disease such as epiretinal membrane or subretinal fluid, or occasionally cortical or migrainous phenomena. The Pulfrich phenomenon is also an illusion, an apparent elliptical path of a truly pendular movement caused by asymmetric conduction delay between the two optic nerves, most often after optic neuritis.

Atropine is the antidote and must be drawn up and immediately available before the test is performed, together with cardiac monitoring. Because of these risks the edrophonium test has largely been replaced in practice by the ice pack test, rest test, and serologic testing for acetylcholine receptor and MuSK antibodies.

question: you are preparing a pathology sample for an eye that underwent enucleation for probable choroidal melanoma. Which of the following represents the appropriate processing with formalin fixative?

options.A: suspend entire eye in formalin for at least 12 hours prior to processing
options.B: section the eye so that the greatest diameter of tumor is within the "po section" and suspend this section in formalin for at least 12 hours
options.C: suspend the entire eye in formalin for no more than 12 hours
options.D: make a small opening at the equator of the eye through which formalin is instilled directly into the eye for at least 24 hours

explanation: You should not open the eye at all prior to soaking it in formalin. If you open the eye and expose it to formalin, you risk damaging and/or distorting sites of pathology. Ideally, the entire eye should be suspended in formalin for at least 12 hours prior to processing (usually: >24 hours). This time period will allow the formalin to diffuse slowly to fix the entire specimen without causing collateral damage. A good way to remember this is that formalin permeates at a rate of ~1 mm/hour. Since the eye is ~24 mm in diameter and the formalin needs to travel 12 mm from each surface to reach the center, it takes 12 hours to fix a globe.

review.explanation: The globe must be fixed intact, suspended whole in formalin for at least 12 hours and in practice usually 24 to 48 hours, before it is opened or sectioned. Formalin penetrates tissue at roughly 1 mm per hour, so a 24 mm globe needs about 12 hours for the fixative to reach the centre from each surface. Opening the eye before fixation, whether by sectioning through the tumour or by injecting formalin through an equatorial window, collapses the globe, distorts and artefactually detaches the retina and tumour, and destroys the architectural relationships pathologists rely on to assess scleral and optic nerve invasion. Limiting fixation to under 12 hours would leave the specimen incompletely fixed and prone to autolysis during sectioning.

These stains matter most for poorly differentiated tumours, where routine processing dissolves the lipid and the tumour can be mistaken for squamous or basal cell carcinoma.
